references.text: Terah took Abram and his family from Ur of the Chaldeans toward Canaan, but they settled in Haran. This is the immediate background for God's call to Abram to leave his country.
The Lord reminds Abram that it was He who brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans to give him the land of Canaan as a possession, thus confirming both the call and the promise of the land.
God repeats the promise to Isaac and refers to Abraham's obedience to God's commands, statutes, and laws—an obedience that began with his response to God's call to leave his homeland.
God renews the land promise to Jacob and confirms the covenant that was initiated when Abram was called to go to the land God would show him.
Isaiah refers to Abraham, who was called alone, blessed, and made numerous—a direct reference to the call where God summoned Abram out of his country.
In his speech, Stephen recounts that the God of glory appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia and told him to leave his country and his relatives, a direct retelling of God's call to Abram.
Paul refers to the promise God gave Abraham and argues that Gentiles are also heirs of the blessing through faith, just as Abraham believed God when he was called.
The book of Hebrews highlights Abraham's obedience as an example of faith: by faith he obeyed the call and went out without knowing where he was going.
Direct retelling and quotation of the same calling event in a New Testament context.
Theological connection between the promise of the land to Abraham and the people's call to take possession of it.
Complementary scenes: the call to go to the land and the subsequent confirmation of the land after arrival.
Theological symmetry: the call to leave the house of one's fathers (Abram) and the call to return to them (Jacob).
Precursor and fulfillment: the call to go to the land and the formal covenant to give the land to his offspring.
Fulfillment of the promise: the call to Abraham and the leading of the people into the promised land.
Direct narrative follow-up: the call to depart and the first confirmation of the promise concerning the land.
Theological contrast: The call to go to Canaan and the prohibition against fleeing to Egypt.
Theological explanation: Why the promise of the land in 12:1 was not fulfilled immediately, but awaited foreign oppression.
Continuity of the promise: Confirmation that the land given to Abraham's offspring is the same as what was promised in 12:1.
Parallel in the patriarchs' lives: God's call for Jacob to return to his fathers' land, mirroring Abraham's call.
Continuity of the promise: Confirmation that the land given to Abraham is also given to Jacob and his descendants.
Fulfillment of the promise: The call to Abraham and the exhortation to the nation to take possession of the land.
Theological contrast: The promise of the land (12:1) and the warning against forsaking God in this land.
